title: EU Gives Caribbean Nations Until 2028 to End Citizenship-for-Sale Programs or Lose Schengen Access
excerpt: The European Commission has formally demanded that five Eastern Caribbean states phase out their citizenship-by-investment programs by June 2028, with interim vetting measures due by September this year.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • EU demands five Caribbean nations end citizenship-by-investment programs by June 2028.
  • Operating a CBI program can revoke Schengen visa-free access for citizens.
  • Antigua's CBI program generated over US$500 million since 2013, vital for its economy.
  • Interim vetting measures must be implemented by September 2026.
  • Caribbean nations face increasing restrictions on visa-free access from multiple countries.

  • The European Commission has demanded that five Caribbean nations — Antigua & Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Saint Lucia — end citizenship-by-investment programs by June 1, 2028.
  • Under the EU's revised visa suspension mechanism, operating a CBI program now constitutes grounds for revoking Schengen visa-free access regardless of program quality.
  • Antigua's Prime Minister warns visa-free access could be lost before the end of 2026 but refuses to phase out a program that has generated over US$500 million since 2013.
  • Interim vetting measures must be in place by September 2026, with the EU's next assessment due in December.

The European Commission has delivered a blunt ultimatum to five Caribbean governments: wind down your citizenship-by-investment programs by June 1, 2028, or risk losing visa-free access to the Schengen Area for all your citizens.

Antigua & Barbuda's Office of the Prime Minister disclosed the demand on Monday, releasing details of a letter from Magnus Brunner, the EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration. Dated June 25, 2026, the letter invokes the EU's revised visa suspension mechanism, which entered into force on December 30, 2025, as the legal basis for the deadline.

Under that framework, the mere operation of a citizenship-by-investment program — "regardless of how well it is managed" — now constitutes "a self-standing ground for suspending visa-free access" to Europe's borderless zone, according to Antigua's statement.

Five Nations, One Deadline

The letters were sent to all five Eastern Caribbean states that run active CBI programs: Antigua & Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Saint Lucia. None of the other four governments had publicly confirmed receipt at the time of Antigua's disclosure.

The Commission offered a 24-month transition period and proposed interim measures: full exclusion of individuals subject to EU sanctions from all CBI applications and reinforced vetting for all nationalities, both to be in place by September 2026.

Antigua Refuses to Blink

Prime Minister Gaston Browne responded with defiance. His government, the statement declared, "will not be pressured into a unilateral phase-out that would cause irreparable harm to the national economy and the welfare of our citizens."

The stakes are substantial. Antigua's CBI program has generated more than EC$1.4 billion — approximately US$518 million — since its launch in 2013. The 2026 budget projects EC$157 million (about US$58 million) in CBI revenue for the year, one of the government's largest non-tax revenue sources. The programs have funded hospitals, schools, infrastructure, and disaster recovery across the islands.

"With or without those visa-free arrangements, our CIP program continues."

— Gaston Browne, Prime Minister of Antigua & Barbuda

The government welcomed the EU's offers of development support through the Global Gateway Investment Agenda but noted pointedly that none of those proposals were "quantified, binding, or explicitly framed as replacement revenues for the CBI income stream."

A Pattern of Closing Doors

The Caribbean programs have been losing visa-free privileges for years. Canada revoked entry for Antiguan CBI passport holders in 2017. The United States imposed restrictions on several visa categories from January 2026. Ireland stripped Saint Lucia and Saint Kitts of visa-free access earlier this year, following similar moves against Dominica and Vanuatu in 2023-2024.

The EU itself permanently revoked Vanuatu's visa waiver in December 2024 over concerns about its golden passport program, after a process that began with a partial suspension in 2022. The December 2025 reform codified the escalating diplomatic threat into binding policy: the European Parliament backed the measure in October, the Council adopted it the following month, and the Commission's eighth Visa Suspension Mechanism report singled out the five Eastern Caribbean programs by name.

What It Means for Investors

Patrick Peters, CEO of investment migration advisory firm Clientreferrals, argued that the deadline is more negotiating tactic than immediate action. "If they wanted to cancel visa-free access, they could do so today. They didn't," he noted, pointing to the two-year window that allows continued talks.

He highlighted the EU's forthcoming ETIAS electronic travel authorization system as a potential compromise — similar to Canada's ETA system, which restored controlled visa-free access for Antiguan and St Kitts citizens in 2023 by screening applicants electronically.

For the thousands of Indian, Chinese, and Middle Eastern nationals who have obtained Caribbean citizenship primarily for travel mobility, the calculus is shifting. A Caribbean passport that once opened doors to 140-plus countries now faces an uncertain future in Europe — the destination that made these programs attractive in the first place.

The September Test

The nearest checkpoint is September 2026, when the EU expects its interim vetting measures to be operational. Antigua & Barbuda's response will feed into the Commission's next Visa Suspension Mechanism report in December 2026, which will determine whether the threat escalates from deadline to enforcement.

A formal deadline now sits where an open-ended threat used to be. Whether it leads to the end of Caribbean golden passports or a negotiated middle ground will depend on what happens in the next five months.
